summary:
We developed a browser-playable educational game (Unity 6, WebGL) where players design and fly an Artemis-style crewed mission to lunar orbit. At a planning desk they choose a launch vehicle and spacecraft parts in an in-game shop with a fixed budget, pick and train a crew of three, choose a launch date from a weather calendar, and complete a launch checklist. Their choices feed a real rocket-equation (delta-v) model built on public NASA reference data, so mass, propulsion, budget and weather become real trade-offs.

The flight then plays out in three phases (departure, lunar orbit, return) with random events and short minigames for each crew role: piloting by timing commands, repairing ship systems, photographing lunar science targets and beaming the data home, and rewiring systems. Poor performance can cause failures, aborts or recovery attempts. A results screen scores planning and execution from 0 to 100, explains what went wrong, and keeps a local top-10 leaderboard.

The project addresses the mission design challenge by letting anyone experience the full loop of planning, simulating and evaluating a space mission under real constraints. It matters because it turns abstract engineering decisions into hands-on choices with visible consequences, making mission design accessible and engaging for students and the public.
details:
Space Mission Simulator Astra is an educational game that lets players experience the full process of planning and flying a space mission, from managing limited resources to launch and the review of the results. Modeled on an Artemis-style crewed lunar orbit mission, it turns decisions that usually stay hidden behind engineering teams into something anyone can try.

The intended impact is to show how every stage of a mission depends on the one before it. During planning, players learn that every part they buy adds mass, that mass limits how much Δv the rocket can deliver, and that these limits decide whether the mission is even possible. They also choose a crew and its training, and a launch site and date, which shows that people and weather are real mission factors alongside hardware. At launch, those earlier decisions come back as consequences: a rocket that is too heavy, an underprepared crew or bad weather raises the risk of problems during flight, and players have to respond to them in real time. In the final review, the score breaks down how each decision affected the result and explains why, so players can see the cause and effect of their choices and apply that thinking to their next mission.

By covering the whole cycle (resources, planning, execution and evaluation), the project helps students, educators and space enthusiasts understand the real trade-offs of mass, power, weather and budget. It also gives teachers a way to talk about systems engineering and mission design without needing a technical background. It is creative because it replaces a spreadsheet-style simulator with a desk and a mission control room, so learning happens through play. The team’s main considerations were educational accuracy, a short play session (about 5–10 minutes), and accessibility, so the game is built to run in the browser.

The game is built in Unity 6 with C#, uses a low poly style, and is designed for WebGL so it can be played without installing anything.
